name: Stable marriage: an instance of size n with more stable matchings than the best known (OEIS A357271 and the Ong et al. 2025 instances)
compute_profile: laptop-hours (exact counting through the rotation poset is fast at these sizes; the search is local search over preference lists, embarrassingly parallel)
statement: An instance of the stable marriage problem of size n consists of complete strict preference lists for n men and n women; a perfect matching is stable if no man and woman prefer each other to their partners. How many stable matchings can an instance of size n have? Finding the maximum f(n) is a research problem posed by Knuth (Mariages Stables, 1976) and repeated by Gusfield and Irving (The Stable Marriage Problem: Structure and Algorithms, 1989, Open Problem 1). Exact values are known only for n <= 5 (OEIS A357269: 1, 2, 3, 10, 16; a(5) = 16 by Eilers with a MiniZinc model), and Thurber (Discrete Mathematics 248, 2002) proved f(n) strictly increasing; the best general upper bound is Palmer and Pálvölgyi's 3.55^n (arXiv:2011.00915). OEIS A357271 (Dan Eilers, 2022) lists lower bounds for n = 1..28 from Thurber's composition constructions (Appendix C of his 2002 paper): 1, 2, 3, 10, 16, 48, 71, 268, 330, 1000, 1231, 6472, 6720, 20176, 25011, 195472, 200832, 456300, 637336, 3419680, 3506880, 11221136, 15481956, 126112960, 127885440, 262860800, 384418176, 2000043808; a(6), a(8), a(10), a(12) and a(16) are conjectured exact. A file linked from A357271 (Ong, Ang, Ho, Eilers, Marks and Buzi, IFoRE 2024 poster 'Improved Hill Climbing for the Stable Marriage Problem'; the file is dated 2024-11-01 and OEIS labels the link 2025) gives explicit instances that raise the bounds for odd n: 81 (n = 7), 365 (n = 9), 1690 (n = 11), 7123 (n = 13) and 27059 (n = 15). Those gains of 6% to 37% came from plain hill climbing, which suggests that the composition bounds for the other cells are soft. Results for this target may also appear as claims in this repository (known-knowns/ and open claim pull requests); they count as published values for the comparison.
success_criterion: Success means explicit preference lists for some n >= 6 (n men and n women, each list a permutation of the other side) whose number of stable matchings, counted exactly by two independent methods that agree, is STRICTLY GREATER (direction: max) than the best known value for that n at verification time: the maximum of the A357271 data line, the instance file linked from A357271 (a357271_1.txt), any other OEIS entry or b-file listing a larger count for that n, any later paper or preprint (search arXiv and the web for the maximum number of stable matchings), and any value for that n recorded in this repository (known-knowns/, TROPHY_CASE.md) or in an open claim pull request. One cell per claim. A count above a value conjectured exact on A357271 (n = 6, 8, 10, 12, 16) would refute that conjecture and needs an extra independent recount. Submitting a new value to OEIS is an action for a human.

partial_wins.statement: A certified exact maximum for n = 6 (extending A357269): a proof that no instance of size 6 has more stable matchings than the best known value, given as a proof object accepted by a formally verified checker (for example an LRAT proof checked by cake_lpr, or a VeriPB proof) for a constraint model whose correctness is argued in a short note, with symmetry breaking proved sound.

verification_method: Parse the 2n preference lists (or the ranking-table format of the A357271 instance file) and check that each list is a permutation. Count stable matchings with two programs that share no code: (1) the Irving-Leather method, i.e. compute the man-optimal stable matching, its rotations and the rotation poset, and count the closed subsets (down-sets) of the poset; (2) an independent enumeration, for example Gusfield's breakmarriage recursion, or brute force over perfect matchings with a stability check for n <= 10. Calibrate both on A357269 (n <= 5), on the published Ong et al. instances (81, 365, 1690, 7123 and 27059 must be reproduced exactly) and on random instances. Re-fetch A357271, its linked file and the repository before claiming.
angles: Hill climbing with exact recounting: the count is a function of the rotation poset, so a move that swaps two entries of one preference list can be re-scored quickly by recomputing rotations; run many diversified restarts in parallel, as the Ong et al. gains suggest.

Grow structure instead of searching blind: Thurber's composition multiplies counts of smaller instances (that is where A357271 comes from), and Latin-marriage constructions give many stable matchings; seed local search with compositions of the best small instances and with Latin-square-based instances, then perturb.

Search the rotation poset directly: many down-sets need wide, shallow posets with few comparabilities; look for preference structures that realise such posets for the target n, then repair them into valid complete preference lists.
Aim at cells where the table value is a plain composition bound (odd n above 15, n >= 17) rather than at the cells conjectured exact.
pitfalls: Count exactly: sampling or estimating the number of stable matchings is not a check, and the two counters must share no code.
Instances must be complete strict preference lists with equal numbers of men and women; ties, incomplete lists and the roommates problem are different records.

The A357271 data line is not the whole table: the linked Ong et al. file holds larger values for n = 7, 9, 11, 13, 15, and other entries (for example A371810) or newer papers may hold more; compare against every source.
A count above a value conjectured exact (n = 6, 8, 10, 12, 16) is more likely a counting bug than a refutation; recount independently before claiming.
